conclusions.answer: The bundled interpreter is CPython 3.12.x, matching /usr/lib/python3.12/argparse.py exactly. Two fingerprints confirm it: (a) help heading is 'options:' (3.10+), and (b) a trailing bare '--' is REPORTED as 'unrecognized arguments: --' rather than being silently dropped (fixed in later 3.12.x/3.13). Also 3.12-specific: help invocation renders '-h, --help' (not the 3.13 '-h, --help' variant with shared metavar) and _get_values only strips '--' for positionals (`if not action.option_strings and action.nargs not in [PARSER, REMAINDER]`).
conclusions.implementation_note: Do not port from memory of a different Python. Every behavior below was verified against /usr/lib/python3.12/argparse.py and the binary.

conclusions.topic: Q1 — Is a '-'-leading token an option or a value? (_parse_optional, exact 9-step order)
conclusions.answer:
argparse classifies EVERY token once, up front, into 'O' (option) or 'A' (value/positional) via _parse_optional (argparse.py:2287-2333). Steps in order: (1) token === '' -> A. (2) token[0] not in prefix_chars ('-') -> A. (3) exact hit in _option_string_actions ('-h','--help','--a','--b','--c') -> O, explicit_arg=null. (4) token.length === 1 (i.e. bare '-') -> A. (5) split at FIRST '=': if prefix-before-'=' is a known option string -> O with explicit_arg = rest. (6) _get_option_tuples abbreviation search (allow_abbrev default True): for '--xxx' tokens, every registered option string that startsWith(prefix-before-'=') is a candidate; for '-x' tokens, candidates are (a) exact 2-char short prefix match with the tail as explicit_arg, and (b) options that startWith the whole token. >1 candidate -> error 'ambiguous option: TOK could match A, B'; exactly 1 -> O. (7) _negative_number_matcher = /^-\d+$|^-\d*\.\d+$/ : if it matches AND _has_negative_number_optionals is empty -> A. (8) token.includes(' ') -> A. (9) otherwise -> O with action=null ('looks like an option, unknown to this parser').

Why '-5' is a value but '-x' is not: both fail steps 3-6. At step 7, '-5' matches ^-\d+$ and this parser registers no option string that itself looks like a negative number, so _has_negative_number_optionals stays [] and '-5' is reclassified as a VALUE ('A'). '-x' matches neither alternation branch, contains no space, so it falls to step 9 and becomes an unknown OPTION ('O'). Since --a's value pattern only accepts 'A' (see Q2), '--a -x' then fails with 'expected one argument'.

_has_negative_number_optionals: populated in _ActionsContainer._add_action (argparse.py:1533-1535) — it gets [True] only if some registered option_string itself matches the negative-number regex (e.g. add_argument('-1')). With options -h/--help/--a/--b/--c it is permanently []. So the port can hardcode 'no negative-number optionals'.

Measured boundary cases (all verified): '-5' A, '-05' A, '-0' A, '-9999999999' A, '-5.5' A, '-.5' A, '-.0' A  ==> accepted as values; '-5.' O, '-1e5' O, '--5' O ('^-\d+$' allows only ONE leading dash), '-x' O ==> 'expected one argument'. '-x y' and ' -x' are values (space rule / not-prefix rule). '-' alone is a value (step 4). '' is a value (step 1).
conclusions.implementation_note: JS: const NEG = /^-\d+$|^-\d*\.\d+$/; test the RAW token. Note ^-\d*\.\d+$ requires digits AFTER the dot and allows none before, so '-.5' passes and '-5.' fails. Classify all tokens BEFORE consuming anything; the classification never changes later.

conclusions.topic: Q2 — 'expected one argument' vs 'unrecognized arguments' (the pattern-match rule)
conclusions.answer:
After classification, argparse builds a string arg_strings_pattern, one char per token: 'O' for options, 'A' for values, and '-' for a literal '--' token (argparse.py:1969-1990). Then _get_nargs_pattern(action) yields a regex: for nargs=None it starts as '(-*A-*)' BUT the last two lines (argparse.py:2415-2417) do `if action.option_strings: pattern = pattern.replace('-*','').replace('-','')` — so for an OPTIONAL with nargs=None the pattern is exactly '(A)'. For the help action (nargs=0) it becomes '()'.

Rule: in consume_optional (argparse.py:2020-2098), for an option with no explicit '=' argument, argparse regex-matches '(A)' against arg_strings_pattern.slice(i+1) anchored at the start. If the very next token was classified 'A' it is consumed as the value; otherwise _match_argument raises ArgumentError -> 'argument --X: expected one argument' (exit 2). So: 'expected one argument' fires when the option is RECOGNIZED but the token immediately after it is not classified 'A' (it is 'O', or '-', or the option is last). 'unrecognized arguments' fires only at the very END, in parse_args, for every token that ended up in the `extras` list — i.e. tokens classified 'O' whose action is null (unknown options), and tokens classified 'A' that no positional could absorb (this parser has zero positionals, so ALL leftover 'A' tokens go to extras).

Equivalently, for this parser: 'expected one argument' = a local, immediate, per-option failure raised during left-to-right consumption; 'unrecognized arguments' = a deferred, global, end-of-parse report. The immediate error always wins if it occurs earlier in the scan (e.g. '--a -x --d 4' reports 'argument --a: expected one argument', never the --d extra).

The action name in the message is _get_action_name(action) = action.option_strings.join('/') (argparse.py:52-63 + ArgumentError.__str__). For --a/--b/--c that is '--a'/'--b'/'--c'; for the help action it is '-h/--help' — so '--help=x' errors as "argument -h/--help: ignored explicit argument 'x'". This was a real bug in my first port; the message never uses the option string the user typed.
conclusions.implementation_note: Implement literally: `if (pattern[i+1] !== 'A') die(`argument ${NAME[action]}: expected one argument`)` where NAME maps action -> option_strings.join('/'). Keep one `extras` array appended to in original order and only report it after the required-check.

conclusions.topic: Q3 — Why '-a 1 --b 2 --c 3' says 'required: --a' (parse_known_args / parse_args split + ordering)
conclusions.answer:
parse_args (argparse.py:2427-2432) is a thin wrapper:
  args, argv = self.parse_known_args(...); if argv: self.error('unrecognized arguments: %s' % ' '.join(argv)); return args
All of the real work — including the REQUIRED check — happens INSIDE _parse_known_args, which returns (namespace, extras). The required check is at argparse.py:2168-2188, i.e. AFTER extras have been collected but BEFORE _parse_known_args returns. So parse_args never gets a chance to report extras when something required is missing: parser.error() calls sys.exit(2) from inside _parse_known_args.

Trace for '-a 1 --b 2 --c 3': '-a' -> step 6 finds no candidate ('-h' and '--help' don't startWith '-a'; '--a' starts with '--', not '-a'), not a negative number, no space -> step 9 -> classified 'O' with action=null. consume_optional sees action===null, pushes '-a' to extras, returns i+1. '1' is classified 'A'; with zero positionals consume_positionals consumes nothing, so '1' is also pushed to extras. --b and --c bind normally. At the required check, seen_actions lacks the --a action -> required_actions = ['--a'] -> error 'the following arguments are required: --a', exit 2. extras (['-a','1']) is discarded. Identical for '--A 1 ...' (matching is case-sensitive; nothing startsWith '--A').

ORDERING RULE, exhaustive and confirmed by fuzzing: (1) errors raised token-by-token during consumption (expected one argument / ignored explicit argument / ambiguous option) — earliest offending token wins; the -h/--help action also FIRES here, printing help and exiting 0; then (2) required-arguments check, joining missing names with ', ' in the order the actions were ADDED (so '--a, --b, --c', never sorted or input order); then (3) mutually-exclusive group check (n/a); then (4) unrecognized arguments, joined with a single ' '.
conclusions.implementation_note: Structure the port as: classify -> consume loop (may exit here) -> required check -> extras check -> print '3\n'. Never merge steps 2 and 4.

conclusions.topic: Q4 — Usage string generation and optional ordering
conclusions.answer:
HelpFormatter._format_usage (argparse.py:296-402) with prefix='usage: '. Actions are partitioned by `if action.option_strings` into optionals and positionals, then _format_actions_usage(optionals + positionals) — optionals ALWAYS first, each group in the order the arguments were ADDED. add_help=True registers -h/--help first (in ArgumentParser.__init__, before any user add_argument), so the order is -h, --a, --b, --c.

Per action: metavar defaults to _get_default_metavar_for_optional(action) = action.dest.upper(). dest for '--a' is 'a', so metavar is 'A'. nargs=None -> args_string is just the metavar. part = optionstrings[0] + ' ' + args_string. If nargs==0 (help), part = optionstrings[0] alone. Then `if not action.required and action not in group: part = '[' + part + ']'`. -h is not required -> '[-h]'; --a/--b/--c are required=True -> bare, NO brackets.

Result: action_usage = '[-h] --a A --b B --c C', usage = prog + ' ' + action_usage, and format_usage() returns 'usage: ' + usage + '\n\n', which format_help() then normalizes (collapse 3+ newlines to 2, strip leading/trailing newlines, append exactly one '\n'). print_usage therefore emits exactly: 'usage: test11.mjs [-h] --a A --b B --c C\n'.

Wrapping (only if 'usage: '.length + usage.length > text_width, text_width = width - current_indent = width): opt_usage is re-split with /\(.*?\)+(?=\s|$)|\[.*?\]+(?=\s|$)|\S+/g, which yields SEVEN parts ['[-h]','--a','A','--b','B','--c','C'] — note '--a A' splits into two independent parts, so a wrap can land between an option and its metavar. If 'usage: '.length + prog.length <= 0.75 * text_width, indent = ' '.repeat(7 + prog.length + 1) and lines = get_lines([prog, ...optParts], indent, prefix) with lines[0] having the indent sliced off; else prog goes on its own line with indent = ' '.repeat(7). get_lines is greedy: line_len starts at (prefix ?? indent).length - 1, and a part is pushed to a new line when line_len + 1 + part.length > text_width and the current line is non-empty; line_len += part.length + 1.
conclusions.implementation_note: For prog='test11.mjs' the one-line form is 40 chars and never wraps at the default width 78; wrapping only matters if COLUMNS < 42. Implementing get_lines verbatim is ~15 lines and makes the port width-exact — I verified byte equality at COLUMNS 25/30/38/45/60/80/200.

conclusions.answer: ArgumentParser.__init__ (argparse.py:1799-1801): `if prog is None: prog = os.path.basename(sys.argv[0])`. sys.argv[0] is the script path as invoked. For the frozen binary that is './test11_executable' -> 'test11_executable'. For the JS port, sys.argv[0] maps to process.argv[1] (the script path; process.argv[0] is the node executable), so PROG = basename(process.argv[1]) = 'test11.mjs'. prog is used verbatim in the usage line and as the 'PROG: error: ...' prefix.
conclusions.implementation_note: Use Python's basename semantics, not node's: `const p = process.argv[1] ?? ''; const PROG = p.slice(p.lastIndexOf('/') + 1);`. path.basename('/x/y/') returns 'y' in node but '' in Python — the manual slice matches Python. Compute PROG once at startup and never hardcode 'test11.mjs'.

conclusions.answer:
Splitting happens in _parse_optional step 5 via str.partition('='), which splits at the FIRST '=' only: arg_string.partition('=') -> (before, '=', after). If `before` is a registered option string, the tuple (action, before, '=', after) is returned, so explicit_arg = everything after the first '=' — it may itself start with '-', contain '=', or be empty.

In consume_optional, when explicit_arg !== null, argparse calls _match_argument(action, 'A') — it forces the literal pattern 'A', completely bypassing token classification. Since --a's pattern is '(A)', arg_count is 1 and the value is taken as-is. Therefore '--a=-x' IS accepted (args.a === '-x'), '--a=--b' is accepted, '--a=1=2' gives '1=2', '--a=-5' gives '-5', and '--a=' gives the EMPTY STRING '' — which still marks --a as seen, so required is satisfied ('--a= --b 2 --c 3' prints 3).

Contrast the other branch: if arg_count were 0 (nargs=0 option like --help) and an explicit arg was given, argparse raises "ignored explicit argument 'X'" — e.g. '--help=x' -> "argument -h/--help: ignored explicit argument 'x'". For a single-dash zero-arg option with an attached tail (e.g. '-hx'), argparse instead treats it as bundled short options: it takes the help action (which prints help and exits 0) and would push '-x' to extras.

Also note step 3 (exact match) runs BEFORE the '=' split, and abbreviation (step 6) also honors '=': '--he=1' resolves to --help with explicit_arg '1'.
conclusions.implementation_note: Split with indexOf('=') and require the index > 0; take everything after it, do not re-split. Never re-classify explicit_arg — it is always accepted verbatim for a nargs=None option.

conclusions.answer:
In the classification loop (argparse.py:1974-1978) the FIRST token equal to '--' appends '-' to the pattern and then drains the remaining iterator appending 'A' for every subsequent token — so nothing after '--' is ever an option, and additional '--' tokens become plain 'A's. Crucially, in 3.12.3 the '--' token itself is NOT removed from arg_strings: _get_values only strips '--' for POSITIONALS (`if not action.option_strings and ...`, argparse.py:2511-2516), and _get_nargs_pattern strips all '-'/'-*' from optionals' patterns, so an optional can never absorb a '--'.

Consequence for a parser with zero positionals: the '--' and everything after it survive to `extras` and are reported verbatim. Verified: '--a 1 --b 2 --c 3 --' -> 'unrecognized arguments: --'; '... -- x' -> 'unrecognized arguments: -- x'; '... -- --' -> 'unrecognized arguments: -- --'; '--a 1 -- --b 2' -> 'unrecognized arguments: -- --b 2' (note --b after '--' is NOT recognized, so --b/--c go missing only if they hadn't already been supplied — the required check still runs first). And '--a -- 5' -> 'argument --a: expected one argument', because the token after --a has pattern '-', not 'A'.
conclusions.implementation_note: Port literally: on the first token === '--', push '-' then push 'A' for every remaining token and stop the classification loop. Do NOT delete '--' from the token array (that is the later-Python behavior and would produce 'unrecognized arguments: ' with an empty tail or silently succeed).

conclusions.answer:
HelpFormatter.__init__ (argparse.py:173-192): width = shutil.get_terminal_size().columns - 2 (COLUMNS env if it parses to >0, else the tty size, else the 80 fallback when stdout is not a tty -> width 78 under test). Then _max_help_position = min(24, max(width - 20, 4)).

Invocations from _format_action_invocation (argparse.py:583-607): nargs==0 -> option_strings.join(', ') = '-h, --help' (10 chars); otherwise each option string is rendered as 'OPT METAVAR' and joined with ', ' -> '--a A' (5). _action_max_length = max(invocation length) + current_indent(2) = 12.

Per-entry geometry (argparse.py:530-570): help_position = min(_action_max_length + 2, _max_help_position) = min(14, 24) = 14; help_width = max(width - help_position, 11) = 64; action_width = help_position - current_indent - 2 = 10.
  - If action.help is falsy (--a/--b/--c have no help): header = ' '.repeat(2) + invocation + '\n'. No padding at all -> '  --a A\n'.
  - Else if invocation.length <= action_width: header = ' '.repeat(2) + invocation.padEnd(action_width) + '  ' (indent_first = 0). '-h, --help' is exactly 10 = action_width -> '  -h, --help' + '  ' = help text starts at column 14.
  - Else header = ' '.repeat(2) + invocation + '\n' and indent_first = help_position (this is what happens at narrow widths, where _max_help_position shrinks).
  Help text is whitespace-collapsed then textwrap.wrap(text, help_width); line 0 is prefixed with indent_first spaces, continuation lines with help_position spaces.

Section assembly in format_help: usage block, description (None), then each action group as a section titled 'positional arguments'/'options' — a section whose body is empty renders as '' (so no 'positional arguments:' heading appears) — then epilog. Finally 3+ consecutive newlines collapse to 2, the string is stripped of leading/trailing newlines, and exactly one '\n' is appended.

Exact expected bytes (width 78), confirmed via od -c against the binary:
'usage: PROG [-h] --a A --b B --c C\n\noptions:\n  -h, --help  show this help message and exit\n  --a A\n  --b B\n  --c C\n'
conclusions.implementation_note: Help goes to STDOUT with exit 0; usage+error go to STDERR with exit 2 (print_usage(stderr) then 'PROG: error: MSG\n'). The help action fires the instant its token is consumed, so '--help --a', '--a 1 --help', '--h', '--he', '-hx' and '--z --help' all print help and exit 0 even with required args missing or unknown extras present — but '--a --help' does NOT: --a's 'expected one argument' error is raised first because it is the earlier token. Do not describe help as unconditionally winning.

conclusions.topic: Extra — value binding, type=str, repeated options, and the program body
conclusions.answer: nargs=None + action='store' -> _get_values takes arg_strings[0] and applies _get_value (type=str is the identity, and no ArgumentTypeError path is reachable), then setattr overwrites the namespace slot, so the LAST occurrence wins ('--a 1 --a 9' -> '9') and required is satisfied by the first occurrence. Empty-string values are fine and count as 'seen'. Unicode passes through unchanged. The Whoosh body is value-independent: it always adds exactly 3 documents and prints len(results) for an Every() query, and Whoosh's default search limit is 10 >= 3, so successful runs always emit exactly the two bytes 0x33 0x0a. No argument value can change that, including '' and non-ASCII.
conclusions.implementation_note: On the happy path just `process.stdout.write('3\n')` — a single write, no trailing blank line. args.a/b/c never need to reach the search logic for the count to be 3, but do keep them if the port implements Whoosh faithfully.

conclusions.answer: A complete, byte-exact JS reference port lives at /tmp/port/test11.mjs (copies at /tmp/port/test11_executable and /tmp/port/test11_executable.mjs used for name-length-exact diffing). It implements: _parse_optional's 9 steps, the O/A/'-' pattern string, consume_optional with the '(A)'/'()' patterns, explicit-arg handling including the nargs=0 'ignored explicit argument' and short-option-bundling branches, abbreviation with ambiguity detection, extras collection, the required-then-extras ordering, _get_action_name's '/'-join, the full usage get_lines wrapper, and the help geometry with _max_help_position = min(24, max(width-20, 4)). Differential harnesses: /tmp/diff.py (52 curated cases), /tmp/fuzz2.py and /tmp/fuzz3.py (random token vectors with COLUMNS variation). Final tallies: 52/52 and 260/260 with zero mismatches on (stdout, stderr, exit code).
conclusions.implementation_note: Two bugs my first attempt hit, both worth guarding against in the real port: (1) treating -h/--help as needing a following 'A' token (its nargs is 0, pattern '()', so it must bind zero args and fire immediately); (2) using the typed option string instead of option_strings.join('/') in ArgumentError messages, which breaks '--help=x' -> must say '-h/--help'.

risks: Python-version drift is the single biggest trap. In later CPython (3.12.7+/3.13) the bare '--' is stripped from extras, _format_action_invocation renders '-h, --help' differently, and _get_nargs_pattern/_get_values differ. The measured 'unrecognized arguments: --' pins this binary to 3.12.3-era behavior. Port from /usr/lib/python3.12/argparse.py, not from memory or newer docs.

Help/usage output is terminal-width dependent: width = shutil.get_terminal_size().columns - 2, which honors the COLUMNS env var. The stated ground-truth bytes correspond to width 78 (stdout piped, no COLUMNS). If a grader runs under a narrow terminal or sets COLUMNS, both usage wrapping and the help column shift (_max_help_position = min(24, max(width-20, 4))). Implement the width logic rather than hardcoding column 14, or the port diverges outside width 78.

prog length feeds the wrapping decision, and the port's prog ('test11.mjs', 10 chars) differs from the binary's ('test11_executable', 17 chars). At very narrow widths the two will legitimately wrap differently; this is unavoidable and not a port bug. Only compare wrap behavior using equal-length prog names.
'-h/--help' vs '--help' in ArgumentError messages is easy to get wrong and is only exercised by '--help=x' / '-h=1' style inputs, which a thin test suite may miss while a fuzzer will not.

The claim 'help anywhere always wins' in the task brief is not exactly true: '--a --help' errors with 'argument --a: expected one argument' because per-token consumption errors fire in left-to-right order before the help action is reached. Encoding 'scan for -h/--help first, then parse' would produce a wrong result for that input.

Zero positionals is what makes extras equal 'all unconsumed tokens in original order'. If anyone later adds a positional to the port, the real interleaved consume_positionals / _match_arguments_partial machinery (and the '--' stripping inside _get_values for positionals) becomes necessary; the simplification silently breaks.

Byte-exactness of stdout matters: '3\n' only, and help must end with a single trailing newline after '  --c C'. console.log-style double newlines or a BOM would fail an od -c comparison. Likewise error output must go to stderr with stdout completely empty.
Abbreviation is on by default (allow_abbrev=True), so '--h', '--he', '--hel' all resolve to --help. A port that only does exact matching would report these as unrecognized instead of printing help.
